questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3\sqrt{t},\,-\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨2,\,-1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the components of the the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$

$v(t)=⟨${{field-1}},{{field-2}}$⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\sqrt{t},\,-\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t,\int -\frac{4}{\sqrt{t+1}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\sqrt{t}+{C}_{1},-8\sqrt{t+1}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨2,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨2\cdot 0\cdot \sqrt{0}+{C}_{1},-8\sqrt{0+1}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,-1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},-8+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ={C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =-8+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t\sqrt{t}+2,\,-8\sqrt{t+1}+7⟩.
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨1,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨4,3⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨4,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨4,3⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},2+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =2+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨t+3,2t+1⟩.
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1},4⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{C}_{1},4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)+{C}_{1},4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡10,3⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡10 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{10}{2}) \\ {C}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =4+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡5,4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡[5(t+1)],4t-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(5t+5),4t-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{e}^{2t},{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2},\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}{e}^{3}⟩\,.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8{t}^{3},-1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -1\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-t+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨2(1)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,-(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{1},\,-1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=4.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨2{t}^{4}-3,\,-t+4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)^{4}-3,\,-(3)+4⟩ \\  & =⟨159,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}

The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨{t}^{2}-1,1-t⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int ({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t,\int (1-t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t+{C}_{1},t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-3+{C}_{1},3-\frac{{3}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},-\frac{3}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t-6,t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-0-6,0-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,1⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{4}{3}\sqrt[3]{t-2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨-1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨{3}^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{1},\sqrt[3]{(3-2)^{4}}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,1⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=8$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-6t+8,\sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4) & =0\,⇒\,t=2,4, \\ \sqrt[3]{(t-2)^{4}} & =0\,⇒\,t=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=2,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨(3)^{3}-5(3)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,(3)^{2}-4(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-18,-8⟩ & =⟨-18+{C}_{1},\,-3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-5.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{t}^{3}-5{t}^{2},\,{t}^{2}-4t-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{3}-5{t}^{2},\,{t}^{2}-4t-5⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}

$$

\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},2(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨-2+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨1-t,2t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1-t,2t-2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}1-t & =0\,⇒\,t=1, \\ 2t-2=2(t-1) & =0\,⇒\,t=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨1,1⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t,\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=0, \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\,⇒\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=0,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

canonical_examples.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 10, 0\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 10,20\rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨10,0⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 10\,\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨10t+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 10,20\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨10(1)+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,20⟩ & =⟨10+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =10+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
C_2 = 20.
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨10t,\,20⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2{e}^{2t},3{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2t}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v}(1) = \langle e^2, 2e^3 \rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{e}^{2(1)}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3(1)}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{2},2{e}^{3}⟩ & =⟨{e}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,{e}^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=0$ and $C_2 = e^3.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨{e}^{2t},\,{e}^{3t}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{e}^{2(2)},\,{e}^{3(2)}+{e}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{4},\,{e}^{6}+{e}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 1, 2t \rangle, \quad -\infty <        t <        \infty.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 2,0 \rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 2,0\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨2,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have $C_1=1$ and $C_2=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨t+1,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}t+1 & =0\,⇒\,t=-1, \\ {t}^{2}-1=(t+1)(t-1) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t= -1,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
